content: 1. The medical use of marijuana would not pose a significant problem if it were regulated as strictly as other medications with potential for abuse. 2. A survey of oncologists revealed that 44% had illegally recommended marijuana to control vomiting, and 48% stated they would do so if it were legal. Additionally, 54% believed marijuana should be available by prescription. 3. THC has been shown to prevent the formation of arterial blockages, which could have significant implications for cardiovascular health. 4. In a study involving 56 patients who had not responded to other antiemetics, 72% experienced success with marijuana. The study also concluded that smoked marijuana was more effective than oral THC pills. 5. A double-blind controlled study demonstrated a 72% reduction in nausea and vomiting among cancer patients receiving high-dose methotrexate. The study further concluded that smoked marijuana was more effective than oral THC. 6. Three separate studies concluded that marijuana use increases appetite in humans, which could be beneficial in certain medical conditions. 7. Research has shown that smoked marijuana was more beneficial than synthetic THC for some patients undergoing cancer chemotherapy. 8. Frequent marijuana use can lead to airway injury, lung inflammation, and impaired pulmonary defense against infections. For patients with AIDS, habitual marijuana use may increase the risk of life-threatening pulmonary infections due to their compromised immune systems. Additionally, the immunosuppressive effects of THC could potentially accelerate the progression of HIV infection, though this possibility remains unexplored. 9. Few controlled longitudinal studies have been conducted to correlate the immunosuppressive effects of marijuana or cannabinoids with the incidence of infections or viral diseases in humans. Further research is necessary to understand the long-term immunological consequences of marijuana and cannabinoid use, particularly in relation to resistance to infections. 10. In children undergoing cancer chemotherapy, delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) has demonstrated anti-nausea and anti-vomiting effects. 11. THC appears to be an effective antiemetic for many cancer patients receiving chemotherapy, particularly those who do not respond to other antiemetic medications.
